stories.title: How climate change and food insecurity could fuel future conflicts
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5Kw3r El Nino-driven drought has left rice fields in West Java, Indonesia, cracked and dry Image: Donal Husni/NurPhoto/picture alliance Advertisement The world's food system is under growing stress, and new research is pointing to areas where this could lead to conflict. Publié le : 06/09/2026 - 04:10 Modifié le : 06/09/2026 - 09:16 2 min Temps de lecture Le photographe espagnol de l'AFP Luis Tato pose avec son trophée après avoir reçu le prix Visa d'Or News lors de la 38e édition du festival de photographie de presse « Visa pour l'image », à Perpignan, dans le sud de la France, le 5 septembre 2026. © Valentine Chapuis / AFP Par : RFI avec AFP Publicité Lire la suite Le photojournaliste espagnol Luis Tato, qui couvre l'Afrique de l'Est et l'océan Indien pour l'AFP, a reçu samedi à Perpignan le Visa d'or News, plus haute distinction du festival Visa pour l'image, récompensant son travail sur le soulèvement de la génération Z malgache en 2025. À lire aussi Visa pour l'image: les Téhéranais dans le cycle infernal de la guerre Après s'être vu décerner son prix, il a rendu un hommage appuyé au fondateur du festival, Jean-François Leroy, décédé lundi, qui lui avait « donné sa chance » en exposant pour la première fois ses images en 2018 alors qu'il « essayai[t] de [se] tracer un chemin » dans ce milieu. « Personne n'a fait autant pour notre écosystème », a-t-il encore salué. Récompensé pour ses photos des manifestants à Madagascar La génération Z, c'est-à-dire les jeunes adultes de moins de 30 ans, s'est trouvée au cœur de plusieurs mobilisations en 2025, notamment au Népal, au Bangladesh, en Bulgarie et donc à Madagascar, grande île de l'océan Indien où d'importantes manifestations, débutées le 25 septembre et violemment réprimées, ont conduit l'armée à renverser mi-octobre le président Andry Rajoelina. À lire aussi Visa pour l'image: en Syrie, «les blessures du passé se referment lentement» Luis Tato, 37 ans, a passé une dizaine de jours parmi les manifestants qui dénonçaient entre autres la défaillance des services publics, la corruption et les difficultés économiques persistantes. « Je pense que ce mouvement mondial de jeunes qui essaient de redéfinir la démocratie et de faire évoluer leur société constitue une dynamique très intéressante, qui me fascine à la fois en tant que photographe et en tant que personne qui cherche à comprendre le monde dans lequel nous vivons », a confié Luis Tato à l'AFP avant de recevoir son prix.

stories.title: Is Russia proving better at protecting friends than fighting enemies in West Africa?
stories.summary: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, The embrace of Russia by Niger, and other Sahel states, has been seen as a rejection of the post-colonial Western powers By Simi Jolaoso Africa correspondent Published 5 September 2026 When mutinous soldiers seized a strategic military base in Niger's capital last Saturday, the country's ruling junta turned to a foreign partner it has increasingly relied on since coming to power: Russia. Following a night of intense fighting in Niamey, Russia's Africa Corps helped Nigerien loyalist forces to regain control of Air Base 101 at Diori Hamani International Airport. Africa Corps, unlike its predecessor the Wagner Group, is directly under the control of the defence ministry in Moscow. It provides combat support and military training and is thought to have some 200 to 300 men in Niger. Russia's ambassador to Niger, Viktor Voropaev, publicly acknowledged the weekend intervention, saying his country's forces had helped "repress a mutiny". "This is seen as a symbolic victory," according to Beverly Ochieng, senior analyst at Control Risks. "[One] that will continue to put them at the centre of not just the counter-insurgency campaign, but even in the protection and prolongation of military rule." The attempted coup offers perhaps the clearest evidence yet that Africa Corps' role in three Sahel countries extends beyond its stated mission of helping governments fight jihadist insurgencies.

stories.summary: Image source, YEAC Image caption, People watched on anxiously as locals organise a rescue effort By Makuochi Okafor ,Â BBC Africa ,Â Reporting from Lagos Â and Â Karina Igonikon ,Â BBC Pidgin ,Â Reporting from Port Harcourt Published 4 September 2026 At least 37 people have died after inhaling toxic fumes while allegedly stealing petrol from a pipeline in Nigeria's Rivers State, an environmental group in the oil-rich region says. Many are still missing after more than 100 people descended on Okari Jetty in Okrika in small boats to collect the refined fuel under cover of darkness, according to the Youths and Environmental Advocacy Centre (YEAC). The police told the BBC an investigation was ongoing to determine the figures of those affected after people reportedly collapsed - with local reports saying some fell into the Bonny River while others were taken to hospital. Theft from pipelines has been a problem for decades in Nigeria's oil hub. Rivers is one of several states that make up the southern Niger Delta region, a vast area of swamps and wetlands with huge reserves of oil and gas along Nigeria's coast.

When the rains arrive late or stop too soon, cotton farmer Debalkie Abate can no longer depend on the planting calendar he once knew. stories.title: Kenya: Ruto Fires Back At Critics of New Police Uniforms
stories.summary: Kenya: Ruto Fires Back At Critics of New Police Uniforms PCS President William Ruto. 4 September 2026 Capital FM (Nairobi) By Davis Ayega Nairobi — President William Ruto has defended Kenya's new police uniforms amid criticism over the design, saying the change is part of a wider plan to transform the National Police Service. Speaking during the 59th Passing-Out Parade for Administration Police recruits at the National Police College in Embakasi, Nairobi, Ruto said the new uniforms should not be viewed as an isolated project. "The new uniforms for general duty officers that we unveiled last week must be understood within this broader reform program," Ruto said. "It is not a standalone intervention, but part of the comprehensive transformation of the National Police Service arising from the reform process." Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn The President said the uniforms were developed after consultations with police officers and members of the public. According to Ruto, the new design was meant to improve the professional identity of officers while also considering their operational needs and dignity. "The uniform itself emerged from consultation with police officers and with the Kenyan public," he said. He acknowledged that a uniform by itself could not change the police service, but argued that it plays a role in building a more professional force. "A uniform alone cannot transform policing, but professional identity and pride are part of building a modern, disciplined, and effective police service," Ruto said. The President also appeared to welcome scrutiny of the wider police reform programme, saying public resources must be properly accounted for. "And because this entire reform program is undertaken in the public interest and financed with public resources, every aspect of it must withstand scrutiny," Ruto said. "We welcome scrutiny of every decision and every shilling spent." Ruto said Kenyans should ask questions about government decisions but warned against condemning individuals without evidence. "We must demand answers without prejudice, question decisions without condemning people unheard, and expose wrongdoing wherever it exists," he said. "Honest scrutiny strengthens institutions, safeguards public resources, and serves the greater public interest." Ruto said the uniform changes are only one part of a much wider programme covering police pay, welfare, housing, training, equipment, technology and infrastructure.

In what became known as the Sharpeville massacre, police infamously opened fire on thousands of peaceful demonstrators. A bullet is still lodged in Mofokeng's spine, and he has a gentle limp from a gunshot to the leg. "We weren't seen as people," the 86-year-old tells the BBC as he explains the reasons he joined the demonstration on 21 March 1960 against the repressive laws of the white-minority government. "All you were good for was working. You couldn't question them, you were supposed to just do as you're told." The massacre at Sharpeville, which he survived, exposed to the world the violence of the racist apartheid system - yet thanks to an indemnity law passed a year after the killings, none of the perpetrators were ever prosecuted. Mofokeng is now part of a legal case announced on Thursday that will seek to overturn this law.

The killings are linked to rumours that a simple tap on the shoulder can cause a man's genitals to shrink or disappear. They are being fuelled by widespread misinformation on social media. "They were shouting that we had stolen someone's genitals and we didn't have any way to escape because there was a huge crowd," Tanzanian mechanic Boniface Mgala told the BBC about his ordeal in April when he was badly beaten by those convinced he was a genital thief. His experience was similar to those in videos seen by the BBC: men claim that their genital organs - penis and testicles - have vanished or shrivelled after coming into contact with strangers and a mob then demands that alleged perpetrators return what they have supposedly stolen. Such claims are rooted in longstanding fears and superstitions - and are not new on the continent, particularly in communities where belief in witchcraft remains widespread.

Based on a worldwide farming population of 934 million, this means approximately 46% of farmers are being poisoned every year.

Women behind the lens: ‘The women are moving towards the church, but it is not the final destination’ South African artist Puleng Mongale explores how her childhood church still connects her to the women of her family, not through religion but shared history and memory T his image, called Holy Gang, combines an image of a church in my mother’s home town, Fateng-tse-Ntsho, in Free State province, South Africa , with self-portraits of me, multiplied to form a group of women. Although at first glance the women are moving towards the church, it is not the final destination. Positioned higher, beyond the church, is what appears to be a rising sun.

stories.title: Tunisia's activists decry civil society crackdown
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5JrLK Tunisians have been protesting against President Kais Saied this summer, demanding the restoration of democracy and calling for the release of jailed activists and journalists amid a worsening economic and social crisis Image: Jihed Abidellaoui/REUTERS Advertisement "Most civil society organizations are in a state of shock today," Messaoud Romdhani, a Tunisian human rights activist told DW. "Those who criticize the authorities or situation in Tunisia face widespread repression," he explained, adding that "most have been accused of money laundering, which leads to the suspension of their activities." Another Tunisian activist, who spoke with DW on condition of anonymity, also said that increasingly people were thinking twice before speaking in public or even choosing to work on sensitive issues. "What worries me most is the chilling effect: When organizations face suspension and activists face prosecution or detention , the uncertainty itself becomes a form of pressure," he said. Human Rights Watch has also raised the alarm. In its latest report , published Wednesday morning, the international rights watchdog concludes that Saied is attempting to shutter Tunisia's civil society entirely. "It is clear that the authorities are abusing every tool at their disposal to close the space for civil society in Tunisia," the report reads. The watchdog also points out that civil society groups in Tunisia have played a key role in holding power to account, delivering essential services and advocating for people's human rights . "The government has used abusive, arbitrary prosecutions, detentions, financial investigations and suspension of organizations in an attempt to stifle these voices," Bassam Khawaja, a deputy director in the Middle East and North Africa Division at Human Rights Watch and editor of the report, told DW. He added that it was clear the idea was to shut down all opposition and independent voices in the country. "This amounts to a total crackdown on civil society in Tunisia," he said.

stories.title: Somali piracy surges as the impact of the US-Iran war ripples outwards
stories.summary: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Pirates manage to board ships operating a long way from the coast and then guide them closer to the shore By Barbara Plett Usher Africa correspondent Published 29 August 2026 Updated 31 August 2026 A surge in piracy near Somalia has increased threats to shipping already under pressure from maritime blockades and conflict due to the US war with Iran. Two cargo vessels were seized in the Gulf of Aden within four days last week, rising to at least 13 the number of ships attacked since the start of the year and triggering unprecedented drone strikes against the pirates. It is the biggest escalation in hijackings in more than a decade, renewing concern about security in this region vital to international trade. "Piracy is always a crime of opportunity," says Omar Mahmood, a senior Somalia analyst for the International Crisis Group (ICG), "and right now the pirates see an opportunity." That opportunity comes from the impact of the war on regional waterways further north. Iran and the US continue to battle over control of the strategic Strait of Hormuz. And Tehran's Houthi allies in Yemen have imposed a targeted blockade in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which controls access to the Red Sea.

stories.title: How a South African town cleaned up its polluted river using stones, wood and sand
stories.summary: The Water Hub’s filter beds remove nearly 99% of toxins before most of the water is released back into the river, with some held back to irrigate gardens. Photograph: Courtesy of Water Hub View image in fullscreen The Water Hub’s filter beds remove nearly 99% of toxins before most of the water is released back into the river, with some held back to irrigate gardens. Photograph: Courtesy of Water Hub How a South African town cleaned up its polluted river using stones, wood and sand Scientists say system to treat contaminated wastewater offers a model for ensuring food security in a fast-warming climate A ll it took to turn the murky, heavily polluted waters of South Africa’s Stiebeuel River into a resource clean enough for irrigating a community’s vegetable plots was a collection of stones, heat-treated wood and sand. Without chemicals and using renewable energy, researchers from the University of Cape Town are cleaning 36,000 litres of water, polluted by sewage, chemicals, and traces of drugs and medication, every day to make it usable for growing food in a fast-expanding informal settlement along the course of the river. Scientists behind the project think it could be a model for ensuring food security in the climate crisis. “ What we’re doing is taking that water, treating it every day, and some of that water is now being used for growing vegetables, for feeding hungry children and people living in the informal settlement,” says Kevin Winter, one of the researchers behind the Water Hub project in Langrug , near Stellenbosch in South Africa’s Western Cape region.

Photograph: Sipa US/Alamy Sweden ends aid to Liberia in a hammer blow to women’s rights and healthcare Sexual and reproductive services face an uncertain future as the country’s second-largest donor halts support worth hundreds of millions of pounds T he Swedish flag is still flying above the pale blue building overlooking the Atlantic in Liberia’s capital, Monrovia, but the doors of the embassy are now closed to visitors. On 31 August, the Swedish embassy in Liberia ends a presence in the country that dates back to 1961. The billions of kronor of aid that Sweden pipes into the west African country will end on the same day, as sweeping cuts to Swedish development funding come into effect.
